In the museum’s layout, Room 4 is the first gallery off the main entrance and forms part of the **Mycenaean (prehistoric) gold** exhibit, where the mask sits in a glass case among other death‑masks and funerary items recovered from the shaft graves at Mycenae.  

**Museum:** National Archaeological Museum, Athens

The **Mask of Agamemnon** is a gold funerary mask which was discovered at the Bronze Age site of Mycenae in southern Greece. The mask, displayed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "_Mona Lisa_ of prehistory".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere20111%E2%80%932-1)
German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann, who discovered the artifact in 1876, believed that he had found the body of the Mycenaean king Agamemnon, leader of the Achaeans in the ancient Greek epic of the Trojan War, the _Iliad_. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to around the 16th century BC, pre-dating the period of the mythical Trojan War by 300–400 years.

Heinrich Schliemann found the gold funeral mask in 1876 in a shaft tomb designated Grave V, at the site Grave Circle A, Mycenae.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3) A total of eight men were discovered in Grave Circle A,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4) all of whom had weapons in their graves,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-5) but only five had masks; those were in Grave IV and Grave V.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4)
The quantities of gold and carefully worked artifacts indicate honor, wealth and status. The Mask of Agamemnon was named by Schliemann after the legendary Greek king Agamemnon of Homer's _Iliad_. Schliemann took this as evidence the Trojan War was a real historical event.
Portrait of Heinrich Schliemann

The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details chased on later with a sharp tool.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-6) Following his discoveries at the site, Schliemann notified King George I.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-7) He is supposed to have told the king in a telegraph, "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-8) Schliemann later named his son after the legendary king. Close to the end of his life, the archaeologist accepted doubts as to the mask's true owner and is quoted as saying, "So this is not Agamemnon... these are not his ornaments? All right, let's call him Schulze."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-9)
The mask in the National Archaeological Museum
In the latter half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century, the authenticity of the mask has been formally questioned, primarily by William Calder III and David Traill.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere2011176-10)_Archaeology_ magazine has run a series of articles presenting both sides of the debate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-11) By the time of the excavation of the Shaft Graves, the Greek Archaeological Society had taken a hand in supervising Schliemann's work (after the issues at Troy), sending Panagiotis Stamatakis as _ephor_, or director, of the excavation, who kept a close eye on Schliemann.
Proponents of the fraud argument center their case on Schliemann's reputation for salting digs with artefacts from elsewhere. The resourceful Schliemann, they assert, could have had the mask manufactured on the general model of the other Mycenaean masks and found an opportunity to place it in the excavation.

The defending advocate(s) point out that the excavation was closed on November 26–27 for Sunday holiday and rain. It was not allowed to reopen until Stamatakis had provided the work with credible witnesses. The three other masks were not discovered until the 28th. The Mask of Agamemnon was found on the 30th.
A second critique is based on style. The Mask of Agamemnon differs from three of the other masks in a number of ways: it is three-dimensional rather than flat, one of the facial hairs is cut out, rather than engraved, the ears are cut out, the eyes are depicted as both open and shut, with open eyelids, but a line of closed eyelids across the center, the face alone of all the depictions of faces in Mycenaean art has a full pointed beard with handlebar moustache, the mouth is well-defined (compared to the flat masks), the brows are formed to two arches rather than one.
The defense presented prior arguments that the shape of the lip, the triangular beard and the detail of the beard are nearly the same as the mane and locks of the gold lion-head rhyton from Shaft Grave IV. Schliemann's duplicity, they claim, has been greatly exaggerated, and they also claim that the attackers were conducting a vendetta.
Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask is genuine but pre-dates the period of the Trojan War by 300–400 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-12) Others date the contents of the find even earlier, to around 2500 BC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-13)

It is considered one of the greatest museums in the world and contains the richest collection of artifacts from Greek antiquity worldwide.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-1)It is situated in theExarcheiaarea in central Athens between Epirus Street, Bouboulinas Street and Tositsas Street while its entrance is on thePatission Streetadjacent to the historical building of theAthens Polytechnicuniversity.

## History
Giacobbe Giusti, National Archaeological Museum, Athens
The Museum in 1893
The first national archaeological museum in Greece was established by the governor of GreeceIoannis KapodistriasinAiginain 1829. Subsequently, the archaeological collection was relocated to a number of exhibition places until 1858, when an international architectural competition was announced for the location and the architectural design of the new museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)
The current location was proposed and the construction of the museum’s building began in 1866 and was completed in 1889 using funds from theGreek Government, theGreek Archaeological Societyand the society ofMycenae. Major benefactors wereEleni Tositsawho donated the land for the building of the museum, and Demetrios and NikolaosVernardakisfromSaint Petersburgwho donated a large amount for the completion of the museum.
The initial name for the museum was _The Central Museum_. It was renamed to its current name in 1881 byPrime Minister of GreeceCharilaos Trikoupis. In 1887 the important archaeologistValerios Staisbecame the museum’s curator.
DuringWorld War IIthe museum was closed and the antiquities were sealed in special protective boxes and buried, in order to avoid their destruction and looting. In 1945 exhibits were again displayed under the direction ofChristos Karouzos. The south wing of the museum houses theEpigraphicMuseum with the richest collection of inscriptions in the world. The inscriptions museum expanded between 1953 and 1960 with the architectural designs ofPatroklos Karantinos.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-3)

## The building
The museum has an imposingneo-classicaldesign which was very popular in Europe at the time and is in accordance with theclassicalstyle artifacts that it houses. The initial plan was conceived by the architectLudwig Langeand it was later modified byPanagis Kalkoswho was the main architect,Armodios VlachosandErnst Ziller. At the front of the museum there is a largeneo-classicdesign garden which is decorated with sculptures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

## Expansions and renovations
Giacobbe Giusti, National Archaeological Museum, Athens
The building has undergone many expansions. Most important were the construction of a new east wing in the early 20th century based on the plans ofAnastasios Metaxasand the construction of a two-storeyed building, designed byGeorge Nomikos, during 1932–1939.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)These expansions were necessary to accommodate the rapidly growing collection of artifacts. The most recent refurbishment of the museum took more than 1.5 years to complete, during which the museum remained completely closed. It reopened in July 2004, in time for theAthens Olympicsand it included an aesthetic and technical upgrade of the building, installation of a modern air-conditioning system, reorganisation of the museum’s collection and repair of the damage caused by the 1999earthquake. The Minoan frescoes rooms opened to the public in 2005.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-4)On May 2008 the Culture Minister Mihalis Liapis inaugurated the much anticipated collection of Egyptian antiquities and the collection of Eleni and Antonis Stathatos.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-5)Today, there is a renewed discussion regarding the need to further expand the museum to adjacent areas. The prehistoric collection displays objects from theNeolithicera (6800–3000 BC), Early and Mid-Bronze age(3000–2000 BC and 2000 to 1700 BC respectively), objects classified asCycladicandMycenaeanart.

#### Neolithic era and early and mid-Bronze age collection
There are ceramic finds from various important Neolithic sites such asDiminiandSesclofrom middleHelladicceramics fromBoeotia,AtticaandPhthiotis. Some objects fromHeinrich Schliemannexcavations inTroyare also on display.

## Collections
### Prehistoric collection
#### Cycladic art collection
Cycladic collection features the famous marble figurines from theAegeanislands ofDelosandKerosincluding the _Lutist_. These mysterious human representations, which resemble modern art and inspired many artists such asHenry Moore,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-10)came from the 3rd millennium BC old cemeteries of Aegean islands along with bronze tools and containers.

## Collections
### Prehistoric collection
#### Mycenean art collection
Mycenean civilization is represented by stone, bronze and ceramic pots, figurines, ivory, glass and faience objects, goldensealsand rings from the vaulted tombs in Mycenae and other locations in the Peloponnese (TirynsandDendrainArgolis,PylosinMessiniaandVaphioinLakonia). Of great interest are the two golden cups from Vafeio showing a scene of the capture of a bull.

## Collections
### Prehistoric collection
#### Mycenean art collection
##### Heinrich Schliemann finds
Mycenean collection includes also the magnificent 19th-century finds ofHeinrich SchliemanninMycenaefrom theGrave Circle Aand the earlierGrave Circle B. Most notable are the golden funerary masks which covered the faces of deceased Mycenean nobles. Among them, the most famous is the one that was named erroneously as themask of Agamemnon. There are also finds from the citadel ofMycenaeincluding relief stelae, golden containers, glass, alabaster and amber tools and jewels. Other features include an ivory carving of two goddesses with a child, a painted limestone head of a goddess and the famous warrior’s vase dating from the 12th century.

The collection is considered to be one of the best collections ofEgyptian artin the world. #### Mycenean art collection
Mycenean civilization is represented by stone, bronze and ceramic pots, figurines, ivory, glass and faience objects, goldensealsand rings from the vaulted tombs in Mycenae and other locations in the Peloponnese (TirynsandDendrainArgolis,PylosinMessiniaandVaphioinLakonia). ## Collections
### Prehistoric collection
#### Mycenean art collection
##### Heinrich Schliemann finds
Mycenean collection includes also the magnificent 19th-century finds ofHeinrich SchliemanninMycenaefrom theGrave Circle Aand the earlierGrave Circle B. Most notable are the golden funerary masks which covered the faces of deceased Mycenean nobles. Among them, the most famous is the one that was named erroneously as themask of Agamemnon. There are also finds from the citadel ofMycenaeincluding relief stelae, golden containers, glass, alabaster and amber tools and jewels. Other features include an ivory carving of two goddesses with a child, a painted limestone head of a goddess and the famous warrior’s vase dating from the 12th century.

## Collections
### Egyptian Art collection
TheEgyptiancollection dates back to the last twenty years of the 19th century. Notable is the donation of the Egyptian government which in 1893 offered nine mummies of the era of thePharaohs. However, the Egyptian collection is mainly by two donors,Ioannis Dimitriou(in 1880) and of Alexandros Rostovic (in 1904). In total the collection includes more than 6000 artifacts, 1100 of which are available presently for the public. The collection is considered to be one of the best collections ofEgyptian artin the world. The exhibition features rare statues, tools, jewels, mummies, a wooden body tag for a mummy, a stunning bronze statue of a princess, intact bird eggs and a 3000-year-old loaf of bread with a bite-sized chunk missing. The **Mask of Agamemnon** is a gold funerary mask which was discovered at the Bronze Age site of Mycenae in southern Greece. The mask, displayed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "_Mona Lisa_ of prehistory".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere20111%E2%80%932-1)
German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann, who discovered the artifact in 1876, believed that he had found the body of the Mycenaean king Agamemnon, leader of the Achaeans in the ancient Greek epic of the Trojan War, the _Iliad_. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to around the 16th century BC, pre-dating the period of the mythical Trojan War by 300–400 years.
texts.1:
Heinrich Schliemann found the gold funeral mask in 1876 in a shaft tomb designated Grave V, at the site Grave Circle A, Mycenae.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3) A total of eight men were discovered in Grave Circle A,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4) all of whom had weapons in their graves,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-5) but only five had masks; those were in Grave IV and Grave V.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4)
The quantities of gold and carefully worked artifacts indicate honor, wealth and status. The Mask of Agamemnon was named by Schliemann after the legendary Greek king Agamemnon of Homer's _Iliad_. Schliemann took this as evidence the Trojan War was a real historical event.
Portrait of Heinrich Schliemann
texts.2:
The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details chased on later with a sharp tool.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-6) Following his discoveries at the site, Schliemann notified King George I.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-7) He is supposed to have told the king in a telegraph, "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-8) Schliemann later named his son after the legendary king. Close to the end of his life, the archaeologist accepted doubts as to the mask's true owner and is quoted as saying, "So this is not Agamemnon... these are not his ornaments? All right, let's call him Schulze."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-9)
The mask in the National Archaeological Museum
In the latter half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century, the authenticity of the mask has been formally questioned, primarily by William Calder III and David Traill.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere2011176-10)_Archaeology_ magazine has run a series of articles presenting both sides of the debate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-11) By the time of the excavation of the Shaft Graves, the Greek Archaeological Society had taken a hand in supervising Schliemann's work (after the issues at Troy), sending Panagiotis Stamatakis as _ephor_, or director, of the excavation, who kept a close eye on Schliemann.
Proponents of the fraud argument center their case on Schliemann's reputation for salting digs with artefacts from elsewhere. The resourceful Schliemann, they assert, could have had the mask manufactured on the general model of the other Mycenaean masks and found an opportunity to place it in the excavation.
texts.3:
The defending advocate(s) point out that the excavation was closed on November 26–27 for Sunday holiday and rain. It was not allowed to reopen until Stamatakis had provided the work with credible witnesses. The three other masks were not discovered until the 28th. The Mask of Agamemnon was found on the 30th.
A second critique is based on style. The Mask of Agamemnon differs from three of the other masks in a number of ways: it is three-dimensional rather than flat, one of the facial hairs is cut out, rather than engraved, the ears are cut out, the eyes are depicted as both open and shut, with open eyelids, but a line of closed eyelids across the center, the face alone of all the depictions of faces in Mycenaean art has a full pointed beard with handlebar moustache, the mouth is well-defined (compared to the flat masks), the brows are formed to two arches rather than one.
The defense presented prior arguments that the shape of the lip, the triangular beard and the detail of the beard are nearly the same as the mane and locks of the gold lion-head rhyton from Shaft Grave IV. Schliemann's duplicity, they claim, has been greatly exaggerated, and they also claim that the attackers were conducting a vendetta.
Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask is genuine but pre-dates the period of the Trojan War by 300–400 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-12) Others date the contents of the find even earlier, to around 2500 BC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-13)

The**National Archaeological Museum**(Greek:Εθνικό Αρχαιολογικό Μουσείο) inAthenshouses some of the most important artifacts from a variety of archaeological locations aroundGreecefromprehistorytolate antiquity. It is considered one of the greatest museums in the world and contains the richest collection of artifacts from Greek antiquity worldwide.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-1)It is situated in theExarcheiaarea in central Athens between Epirus Street, Bouboulinas Street and Tositsas Street while its entrance is on thePatission Streetadjacent to the historical building of theAthens Polytechnicuniversity.

## History
Giacobbe Giusti, National Archaeological Museum, Athens
The Museum in 1893
The first national archaeological museum in Greece was established by the governor of GreeceIoannis KapodistriasinAiginain 1829. Subsequently, the archaeological collection was relocated to a number of exhibition places until 1858, when an international architectural competition was announced for the location and the architectural design of the new museum.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)
The current location was proposed and the construction of the museum’s building began in 1866 and was completed in 1889 using funds from theGreek Government, theGreek Archaeological Societyand the society ofMycenae. Major benefactors wereEleni Tositsawho donated the land for the building of the museum, and Demetrios and NikolaosVernardakisfromSaint Petersburgwho donated a large amount for the completion of the museum.
The initial name for the museum was _The Central Museum_. It was renamed to its current name in 1881 byPrime Minister of GreeceCharilaos Trikoupis. In 1887 the important archaeologistValerios Staisbecame the museum’s curator.
DuringWorld War IIthe museum was closed and the antiquities were sealed in special protective boxes and buried, in order to avoid their destruction and looting. In 1945 exhibits were again displayed under the direction ofChristos Karouzos. The south wing of the museum houses theEpigraphicMuseum with the richest collection of inscriptions in the world. The inscriptions museum expanded between 1953 and 1960 with the architectural designs ofPatroklos Karantinos.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-3)

## The building
The museum has an imposingneo-classicaldesign which was very popular in Europe at the time and is in accordance with theclassicalstyle artifacts that it houses. The initial plan was conceived by the architectLudwig Langeand it was later modified byPanagis Kalkoswho was the main architect,Armodios VlachosandErnst Ziller. At the front of the museum there is a largeneo-classicdesign garden which is decorated with sculptures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)

## Expansions and renovations
Giacobbe Giusti, National Archaeological Museum, Athens
The building has undergone many expansions. Most important were the construction of a new east wing in the early 20th century based on the plans ofAnastasios Metaxasand the construction of a two-storeyed building, designed byGeorge Nomikos, during 1932–1939.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-Raffy-2)These expansions were necessary to accommodate the rapidly growing collection of artifacts. The most recent refurbishment of the museum took more than 1.5 years to complete, during which the museum remained completely closed. It reopened in July 2004, in time for theAthens Olympicsand it included an aesthetic and technical upgrade of the building, installation of a modern air-conditioning system, reorganisation of the museum’s collection and repair of the damage caused by the 1999earthquake. The Minoan frescoes rooms opened to the public in 2005.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-4)On May 2008 the Culture Minister Mihalis Liapis inaugurated the much anticipated collection of Egyptian antiquities and the collection of Eleni and Antonis Stathatos.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Athens#cite_note-5)Today, there is a renewed discussion regarding the need to further expand the museum to adjacent areas. The **Mask of Agamemnon** is a gold funerary mask which was discovered at the Bronze Age site of Mycenae in southern Greece. The mask, displayed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "_Mona Lisa_ of prehistory".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere20111%E2%80%932-1)
German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann, who discovered the artifact in 1876, believed that he had found the body of the Mycenaean king Agamemnon, leader of the Achaeans in the ancient Greek epic of the Trojan War, the _Iliad_. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to around the 16th century BC, pre-dating the period of the mythical Trojan War by 300–400 years.

Heinrich Schliemann found the gold funeral mask in 1876 in a shaft tomb designated Grave V, at the site Grave Circle A, Mycenae.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3) A total of eight men were discovered in Grave Circle A,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4) all of whom had weapons in their graves,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-5) but only five had masks; those were in Grave IV and Grave V.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4)
The quantities of gold and carefully worked artifacts indicate honor, wealth and status. The Mask of Agamemnon was named by Schliemann after the legendary Greek king Agamemnon of Homer's _Iliad_. Schliemann took this as evidence the Trojan War was a real historical event.
Portrait of Heinrich Schliemann

The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details chased on later with a sharp tool.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-6) Following his discoveries at the site, Schliemann notified King George I.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-7) He is supposed to have told the king in a telegraph, "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-8) Schliemann later named his son after the legendary king. Close to the end of his life, the archaeologist accepted doubts as to the mask's true owner and is quoted as saying, "So this is not Agamemnon... these are not his ornaments? All right, let's call him Schulze."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-9)
The mask in the National Archaeological Museum
In the latter half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century, the authenticity of the mask has been formally questioned, primarily by William Calder III and David Traill.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere2011176-10)_Archaeology_ magazine has run a series of articles presenting both sides of the debate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-11) By the time of the excavation of the Shaft Graves, the Greek Archaeological Society had taken a hand in supervising Schliemann's work (after the issues at Troy), sending Panagiotis Stamatakis as _ephor_, or director, of the excavation, who kept a close eye on Schliemann.
Proponents of the fraud argument center their case on Schliemann's reputation for salting digs with artefacts from elsewhere. The resourceful Schliemann, they assert, could have had the mask manufactured on the general model of the other Mycenaean masks and found an opportunity to place it in the excavation.

The defending advocate(s) point out that the excavation was closed on November 26–27 for Sunday holiday and rain. It was not allowed to reopen until Stamatakis had provided the work with credible witnesses. The three other masks were not discovered until the 28th. The Mask of Agamemnon was found on the 30th.
A second critique is based on style. The Mask of Agamemnon differs from three of the other masks in a number of ways: it is three-dimensional rather than flat, one of the facial hairs is cut out, rather than engraved, the ears are cut out, the eyes are depicted as both open and shut, with open eyelids, but a line of closed eyelids across the center, the face alone of all the depictions of faces in Mycenaean art has a full pointed beard with handlebar moustache, the mouth is well-defined (compared to the flat masks), the brows are formed to two arches rather than one.
The defense presented prior arguments that the shape of the lip, the triangular beard and the detail of the beard are nearly the same as the mane and locks of the gold lion-head rhyton from Shaft Grave IV. Schliemann's duplicity, they claim, has been greatly exaggerated, and they also claim that the attackers were conducting a vendetta.
Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask is genuine but pre-dates the period of the Trojan War by 300–400 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-12) Others date the contents of the find even earlier, to around 2500 BC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-13)

The National Archaeological Museum is the largest archaeological museum in Greece and one of the most significant in the world. Its collection spans roughly 7,000 years of Greek history, from the Neolithic period through late antiquity. That scale is also the problem.
When every room contains world-class objects with three-line placards, everything starts to blur. A Mycenaean gold cup from 1500 BCE sits three meters from a Roman marble portrait from 200 CE with almost identical presentation. Without context, the eye stops distinguishing.
The approach that works is selective. This is not a place to see everything — it's a place to understand six specific things very well. Choose those objects. Know their stories before you walk in. When you stand in front of the Mask of Agamemnon or the Artemision Bronze with the full story already loaded, the experience becomes something different: a confirmation of something you almost already knew, delivered in three dimensions at 1:1 scale.

**Room 4** holds the Mycenaean gold collection — funeral goods excavated by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 from the royal shaft graves at **Mycenae**, the fortified Bronze Age palace city in the Peloponnese. The room contains extraordinary objects: inlaid daggers, ceremonial drinking cups, amber jewelry. In the center case, behind glass, is a hammered-gold funeral mask the size of a human face.
Schliemann sent a telegram to the King of Greece when he found it: *'I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon.'* The name has never left the object.
The mask almost certainly does not show Agamemnon. The man depicted was buried around 1550–1500 BCE, and Agamemnon — if he existed — would have lived around 1250 BCE. The mask predates any plausible Trojan War by 250 to 300 years. What it does show is a specific man: heavy beard, mustache, a face of middle age, eyes closed, features pressed from a single sheet of hammered gold by someone who knew this face well enough to render it with personality rather than convention. He was powerful enough to be buried wearing 450 grams of gold, and someone cared about his face enough to record it.
The Mycenaean civilization left almost no narrative texts — Linear B has been deciphered, but the tablets are administrative records, not history. This mask and the objects around it in Room 4 are among the few things from that world that carry the weight of individual human presence.
Get short, interactive stories that make each place easier to remember while you travel.
Near the end of the sculpture gallery, a bronze figure stands in mid-throw. Both arms are fully extended — one forward, one swept back — in a pose of suspended force. The figure is 2.09 meters tall, clearly divine, and dated to approximately **460 BCE**, the Early Classical period just before the Parthenon.
The statue was found in 1926 and 1928 in the sea off **Cape Artemision**, on the northern tip of the island of Euboea — the same waters where the Greeks and Persians fought a major naval battle in 480 BCE. It had been on a ship that sank during Roman-era transport.

The debate that has never been resolved: if the god is holding a **trident**, he's Poseidon. If he's holding a **thunderbolt**, he's Zeus. Both weapons would have been thin bronze rods, long since lost. The right hand is open. Art historians have been arguing about the width of that grip for ninety years.
What is unambiguous is the technical achievement. The figure's weight rests on one foot, the torso is rotated nearly 90 degrees, and the extended arms create a span of over two meters — all in solid bronze, all in perfect balance. Whoever cast this in the 5th century BCE was working at a level that would not be matched in Europe for roughly 1,500 years. The **Jockey of Artemision**, nearby — a small boy on a full-speed galloping horse, his face straining with effort, circa 150 BCE — came from the same underwater site and is equally worth stopping for.
In 1900, a sponge-diving boat caught in a storm off the small island of **Antikythera** — between Crete and the Peloponnese — dropped anchor in a bay and sent divers down to wait out the weather. One of them surfaced with pieces of bronze. What followed was the first major underwater archaeological excavation in history.
The **Antikythera shipwreck** was a large Roman-era cargo vessel, probably carrying looted Greek art from the Aegean back to Italy. The haul included life-size statues, glassware, pottery, and one object that would not be fully understood for another century.
The most visible survivor, displayed in the sculpture galleries, is the **Youth of Antikythera** — a nearly complete bronze figure, 1.96 meters tall, his right arm extended as if he once held something (an apple? a ball? scholarly opinion is divided). The original eyes were glass or stone, now missing. What remains has a quality of arrested presence — someone caught mid-moment, not posed. It is one of the finest surviving bronzes from the 4th century BCE.
Take the staircase to the **second floor**. In **Room 38**, behind glass, are fragments of corroded bronze that look like they belong in a geology collection. The placard explains what they are: the remains of a **mechanical astronomical calculator** built approximately 100 BCE.

The **Antikythera Mechanism** contained at least 30 interlocking bronze gear wheels inside a hand-sized wooden box, operated by a hand crank. Turning the crank moved pointers on circular dials on the front and back faces. The front dial tracked the positions of the sun and moon in the zodiac. The back dials tracked the **Metonic cycle** (the 19-year alignment of the lunar and solar calendars), the **Saros cycle** (an 18-year eclipse prediction cycle), and a games calendar used to schedule the Olympic and Panhellenic festivals.
In plain terms: it predicted where the sun and moon would be on any future date and told you when the next eclipse would occur, 18 years in advance, correctly.
The nearest comparable European technology — mechanical astronomical clocks using similar gear trains — does not appear until the **14th century CE**. The Antikythera Mechanism is roughly 1,400 years ahead of anything else in the record. A working reconstruction, built by University College London researchers in 2021, stands next to the fragments. The reconstruction rotates. It is the most useful exhibit in the museum, and most visitors never see it.
**Room 48** holds the Thera frescoes — wall paintings from **Akrotiri**, the Bronze Age settlement on Santorini buried when the Thera volcano erupted around 1600 BCE. Akrotiri was a sophisticated trading city: multi-story buildings, indoor plumbing, elaborate painted walls. The ash preserved it for 3,600 years before excavation began in 1967.
The frescoes are remarkable on two grounds. First, the color: the sealed ash environment preserved the mineral pigments at near-full intensity. A painting of swallows in flight from 1600 BCE looks like it was made recently. Second, the subjects: the Akrotiri painters depicted daily life with unusual warmth and specificity. The **'Boxing Children' fresco** shows two boys in gloves sparring, their faces unposed and concentrated. The **'Spring fresco'** shows swallows over red lilies growing from rocky outcrops — a landscape painting, which is a genuinely unusual genre in ancient art.

The people of Akrotiri appear to have evacuated before the eruption — no human remains have been found in the ruins, and no gold was left behind. Someone warned them. Who gave the warning and how the population survived is unknown. The paintings they left on their walls are in Room 48.
**The ceramic galleries** (Rooms 49–56, on the ground and upper floors) are excellent by any specialist standard but visually repetitive without prior knowledge of Greek vase-painting conventions. Spend 10 minutes here rather than 45 unless ceramics are your specific interest.
**The Egyptian and Near Eastern collection** on the ground floor is a curiosity — these objects came to Athens through ancient trade — but is secondary to the Greek material. A glance is enough.
**The audio guide** (€5 extra) covers the Mycenaean and sculpture galleries well, but does not meaningfully cover the Antikythera Mechanism or the Akrotiri frescoes. For Rooms 38 and 48, the display placards are more informative. Skip the guide for those rooms.
**The museum shop**, near the exit, sells a working mini-replica of the Antikythera Mechanism gear model — one of the more legitimate souvenirs available in Athens, since the actual object is housed here. It is not available in most tourist shops.
**When to visit?** In June, the museum is open daily **8 a.m. to 8 p.m.** (Tuesdays from 1 p.m.). Lightest crowds are at opening and the hour before closing. Tour groups typically land between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. The building is fully air-conditioned — one of the few central Athens attractions that is genuinely comfortable at midday in summer, when outdoor temperatures regularly reach 34–36°C.
**How long?** The six-object approach in this guide takes about **2 to 2.5 hours** at a comfortable pace, including time to read placards and move between floors. A full survey of the museum takes 4 to 5 hours and is genuinely tiring. If you are visiting with children, Room 4 (Mycenaean gold) and Room 15 (the Artemision Bronze) are the most immediately striking for first-timers.

**How to get there?** The museum is at **Patission 44**, about 1 km north of Omonia Square. From **Omonia metro** (Lines 1 and 2), walk north along Patission Street — about 10 minutes. From Exarcheia, the neighborhood directly east, it is a 5-minute walk west along Stournari Street. Combining the museum with lunch in Exarcheia is a natural pairing: Kallidromiou Street market and the cafes around Exarcheia Square are 10 minutes on foot from the museum entrance.

Maybe.
A few decades ago, questions were raised about the authenticity of the “mask of Agamemnon” which Heinrich Schleimann (claimed to have) found at Mycenae. The style is notably different from the other masks found at the site. The others have faces which are clean shaven with bulbous features and ears worked into them in a single piece. The Agamemnon mask has a full beard and the ears are separate pieces attached to the main mask. And there are circumstances of the (purported) discovery of the mask which can be framed in a way which makes it sound suspicious. For example, some people have found a resemblance between the mask and pictures of Schleimann himself, and Schleimann’s wife was related to a goldsmith.

# Is it true that the "golden mask of Agamemnon" that is on display in the National Archeological Museum in Athens is fake? Is anything genuine about this country?
Given the lack of other stylistic evidence to compare the masks to, the biggest problem with resolving the question is that it’s difficult to authenticate metal objects. Or rather, there are ways in which their authenticity might be ruled out but not really ruled in. It would be possible, for example, to chemically analyze the mask to see if its composition matches that of more securely identified Mycenaean gold items. However, the mask might have been made from scraps of ancient gold, giving it the same composition. On top of that, museums tend to be generally unenthusiastic about the prospect of establishing that their most prized holdings may be forgeries, so there’s been little activity in that direction.
So, then, the question has been raised based on plausible but not overwhelmingly strong evidence, and there’s no particular urgency on the part of the museum holding the mask to respond to those charges. Don’t look for this to be settled any time soon.

Well, it ain’t Agamemnon.
It is on the first floor of the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, as part of a rather amazing collection of prehistoric * material, including nice Cycladic pieces and earlier, but in a pair of connected rooms that are more-or-less the stuff Schliemann collected from the shaft graves he excavated at Mycenae.
So the collection is, pretty much beyond dispute, full of Mycenaean objects. A whole whole bunch of tiny delicate gold, looking as new as the day it was made, some rather less well preserved (gold is incorruptible) swords, and a fragment of a boar’s tusk helmet.
And a few rhyton and pots that are themselves famous — the Warrior Vase, prime among them — but I want to come back to that helmet.
Because the Mycenae are pre-historic. They did write, or rather they took account books, but the closest we come to a “history” of them is Greek mythology, and particularly the Homeric cycle written (off the top of my head so don’t quote me!) about four hundred years later.

# Is it true that the "golden mask of Agamemnon" that is on display in the National Archeological Museum in Athens is fake? Is anything genuine about this country?
And oh yeah, those shaft grave are older still. If there was a historical “Trojan War,” the graves Schliemann was digging into were from a good four hundred years earlier than that. Which is par for the course with him: at least he didn’t use dynamite this time.
There is controversy about several of the items Schliemann collected. He was pretty much all about controversy. Bragging about stealing from the Turks by hiding the “jewels of Helen” in his young wife’s things… (a story he made up after the fact, at that). So it has been suggested that he may have reworked some of the items to make them look more spectacular.
This is not to cast doubt on the bulk of the collection. There are just too many items there, and too many of them would be all but impossible to fake today, much less in Schliemann’s time. And you really have to visit the museum in person to understand just how much there is there, and how fine and detailed the workmanship is. If he had every goldsmith in Athens working away at it he still couldn’t have faked a hundredth of it, and that’s just the gold items alone.
Aggy’s mask is famous, though. We always like faces, because they seem to speak to us from across the ages. The Fayum portraits have captivated generations, even if there’s some strong evidence that many were mass-produced and not exactly a portrait of the deceased (“Hey, add a little black hair and a mustache on #14, will you? I just talked to the widow.”)
And people are split. Even then, it seemed a little too good to be true. It also is different from other death masks of the same period and circumstance. Some have carried this further and suggested that it was heavily reworked to fit Schliemann’s Germanic preconceptions of a Warrior-King.

Me, I’m on the fence. Pretty much everyone accepts it came out of the ground and is as old as we think it is, and belonged to a (unfortunately un-named and will remain unknown to history) figure of some importance. It seems hard to disagree that it was probably cleaned up and repaired, since objects that have been in the ground, and taken out by workers of the period (with or without dynamite) are likely to be in sorry shape.

## National Archaeological Museum Athens tickets: guided tour or audio guide, and the Tuesday trap
National Archaeological Museum Athens tickets come down to one choice: a two-hour small-group tour with entry from €59, or a plain ticket with an audio guide from €26 that you walk round at your own pace. What the ticket buys is priority access at the entrance and, on the guided option, a licensed guide who takes you straight to the Mask of Agamemnon, the Antikythera Mechanism and the bronze Zeus without a wrong turn in between. Tour groups hit the Mycenaean gold rooms by 10 a.m. The museum opens at 8 a.m. in summer (Tuesday from 1 p.m. — avoid Tuesday mornings). Arrive at 8 and go straight to Room 4. You'll have the Mask of Agamemnon to yourself for about 20 minutes.
The Antikythera Mechanism — a 2,100-year-old astronomical calculator with 30 interlocking gears — is in Room 38 upstairs. Roughly 80% of visitors never make it to the second floor. The corroded fragments look unremarkable; the working reconstruction next to them is one of the most extraordinary objects in the building.
Full admission is €15, reduced €8. Free on the first Sunday of the month from November to March (not in summer). Photography without flash is permitted throughout. The museum is at Patission 44 — nearest metro is Omonia (Lines 1 and 2), then a 10-minute walk north along Patission Street.
The National Archaeological Museum is the largest archaeological museum in Greece and one of the most significant in the world. Its collection spans roughly 7,000 years of Greek history, from the Neolithic period through late antiquity. That scale is also the problem.
When every room contains world-class objects with three-line placards, everything starts to blur. A Mycenaean gold cup from 1500 BCE sits three meters from a Roman marble portrait from 200 CE with almost identical presentation. Without context, the eye stops distinguishing.
The approach that works is selective. This is not a place to see everything — it's a place to understand six specific things very well. Choose those objects. Know their stories before you walk in. When you stand in front of the Mask of Agamemnon or the Artemision Bronze with the full story already loaded, the experience becomes something different: a confirmation of something you almost already knew, delivered in three dimensions at 1:1 scale.
texts.1:
**Room 4** holds the Mycenaean gold collection — funeral goods excavated by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 from the royal shaft graves at **Mycenae**, the fortified Bronze Age palace city in the Peloponnese. The room contains extraordinary objects: inlaid daggers, ceremonial drinking cups, amber jewelry. In the center case, behind glass, is a hammered-gold funeral mask the size of a human face.
Schliemann sent a telegram to the King of Greece when he found it: *'I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon.'* The name has never left the object.
The mask almost certainly does not show Agamemnon. The man depicted was buried around 1550–1500 BCE, and Agamemnon — if he existed — would have lived around 1250 BCE. The mask predates any plausible Trojan War by 250 to 300 years. What it does show is a specific man: heavy beard, mustache, a face of middle age, eyes closed, features pressed from a single sheet of hammered gold by someone who knew this face well enough to render it with personality rather than convention. He was powerful enough to be buried wearing 450 grams of gold, and someone cared about his face enough to record it.
The Mycenaean civilization left almost no narrative texts — Linear B has been deciphered, but the tablets are administrative records, not history. This mask and the objects around it in Room 4 are among the few things from that world that carry the weight of individual human presence.
Get short, interactive stories that make each place easier to remember while you travel.
Near the end of the sculpture gallery, a bronze figure stands in mid-throw. Both arms are fully extended — one forward, one swept back — in a pose of suspended force. The figure is 2.09 meters tall, clearly divine, and dated to approximately **460 BCE**, the Early Classical period just before the Parthenon.
The statue was found in 1926 and 1928 in the sea off **Cape Artemision**, on the northern tip of the island of Euboea — the same waters where the Greeks and Persians fought a major naval battle in 480 BCE. It had been on a ship that sank during Roman-era transport.
texts.2:
The debate that has never been resolved: if the god is holding a **trident**, he's Poseidon. If he's holding a **thunderbolt**, he's Zeus. Both weapons would have been thin bronze rods, long since lost. The right hand is open. Art historians have been arguing about the width of that grip for ninety years.
What is unambiguous is the technical achievement. The figure's weight rests on one foot, the torso is rotated nearly 90 degrees, and the extended arms create a span of over two meters — all in solid bronze, all in perfect balance. Whoever cast this in the 5th century BCE was working at a level that would not be matched in Europe for roughly 1,500 years. The **Jockey of Artemision**, nearby — a small boy on a full-speed galloping horse, his face straining with effort, circa 150 BCE — came from the same underwater site and is equally worth stopping for.
In 1900, a sponge-diving boat caught in a storm off the small island of **Antikythera** — between Crete and the Peloponnese — dropped anchor in a bay and sent divers down to wait out the weather. One of them surfaced with pieces of bronze. What followed was the first major underwater archaeological excavation in history.
The **Antikythera shipwreck** was a large Roman-era cargo vessel, probably carrying looted Greek art from the Aegean back to Italy. The haul included life-size statues, glassware, pottery, and one object that would not be fully understood for another century.
The most visible survivor, displayed in the sculpture galleries, is the **Youth of Antikythera** — a nearly complete bronze figure, 1.96 meters tall, his right arm extended as if he once held something (an apple? a ball? scholarly opinion is divided). The original eyes were glass or stone, now missing. What remains has a quality of arrested presence — someone caught mid-moment, not posed. It is one of the finest surviving bronzes from the 4th century BCE.
Take the staircase to the **second floor**. In **Room 38**, behind glass, are fragments of corroded bronze that look like they belong in a geology collection. The placard explains what they are: the remains of a **mechanical astronomical calculator** built approximately 100 BCE.
texts.3:
The **Antikythera Mechanism** contained at least 30 interlocking bronze gear wheels inside a hand-sized wooden box, operated by a hand crank. Turning the crank moved pointers on circular dials on the front and back faces. The front dial tracked the positions of the sun and moon in the zodiac. The back dials tracked the **Metonic cycle** (the 19-year alignment of the lunar and solar calendars), the **Saros cycle** (an 18-year eclipse prediction cycle), and a games calendar used to schedule the Olympic and Panhellenic festivals.
In plain terms: it predicted where the sun and moon would be on any future date and told you when the next eclipse would occur, 18 years in advance, correctly.
The nearest comparable European technology — mechanical astronomical clocks using similar gear trains — does not appear until the **14th century CE**. The Antikythera Mechanism is roughly 1,400 years ahead of anything else in the record. A working reconstruction, built by University College London researchers in 2021, stands next to the fragments. The reconstruction rotates. It is the most useful exhibit in the museum, and most visitors never see it.
**Room 48** holds the Thera frescoes — wall paintings from **Akrotiri**, the Bronze Age settlement on Santorini buried when the Thera volcano erupted around 1600 BCE. Akrotiri was a sophisticated trading city: multi-story buildings, indoor plumbing, elaborate painted walls. The ash preserved it for 3,600 years before excavation began in 1967.
The frescoes are remarkable on two grounds. First, the color: the sealed ash environment preserved the mineral pigments at near-full intensity. A painting of swallows in flight from 1600 BCE looks like it was made recently. Second, the subjects: the Akrotiri painters depicted daily life with unusual warmth and specificity. The **'Boxing Children' fresco** shows two boys in gloves sparring, their faces unposed and concentrated. The **'Spring fresco'** shows swallows over red lilies growing from rocky outcrops — a landscape painting, which is a genuinely unusual genre in ancient art.
texts.4:
The people of Akrotiri appear to have evacuated before the eruption — no human remains have been found in the ruins, and no gold was left behind. Someone warned them. Who gave the warning and how the population survived is unknown. The paintings they left on their walls are in Room 48.
**The ceramic galleries** (Rooms 49–56, on the ground and upper floors) are excellent by any specialist standard but visually repetitive without prior knowledge of Greek vase-painting conventions. Spend 10 minutes here rather than 45 unless ceramics are your specific interest.
**The Egyptian and Near Eastern collection** on the ground floor is a curiosity — these objects came to Athens through ancient trade — but is secondary to the Greek material. A glance is enough.
**The audio guide** (€5 extra) covers the Mycenaean and sculpture galleries well, but does not meaningfully cover the Antikythera Mechanism or the Akrotiri frescoes. For Rooms 38 and 48, the display placards are more informative. Skip the guide for those rooms.
**The museum shop**, near the exit, sells a working mini-replica of the Antikythera Mechanism gear model — one of the more legitimate souvenirs available in Athens, since the actual object is housed here. It is not available in most tourist shops.
**When to visit?** In June, the museum is open daily **8 a.m. to 8 p.m.** (Tuesdays from 1 p.m.). Lightest crowds are at opening and the hour before closing. Tour groups typically land between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. The building is fully air-conditioned — one of the few central Athens attractions that is genuinely comfortable at midday in summer, when outdoor temperatures regularly reach 34–36°C.
**How long?** The six-object approach in this guide takes about **2 to 2.5 hours** at a comfortable pace, including time to read placards and move between floors. A full survey of the museum takes 4 to 5 hours and is genuinely tiring. If you are visiting with children, Room 4 (Mycenaean gold) and Room 15 (the Artemision Bronze) are the most immediately striking for first-timers.

Maybe.
A few decades ago, questions were raised about the authenticity of the “mask of Agamemnon” which Heinrich Schleimann (claimed to have) found at Mycenae. # Is it true that the "golden mask of Agamemnon" that is on display in the National Archeological Museum in Athens is fake? Is anything genuine about this country?
Given the lack of other stylistic evidence to compare the masks to, the biggest problem with resolving the question is that it’s difficult to authenticate metal objects. Or rather, there are ways in which their authenticity might be ruled out but not really ruled in. It would be possible, for example, to chemically analyze the mask to see if its composition matches that of more securely identified Mycenaean gold items. However, the mask might have been made from scraps of ancient gold, giving it the same composition. On top of that, museums tend to be generally unenthusiastic about the prospect of establishing that their most prized holdings may be forgeries, so there’s been little activity in that direction.
So, then, the question has been raised based on plausible but not overwhelmingly strong evidence, and there’s no particular urgency on the part of the museum holding the mask to respond to those charges. Don’t look for this to be settled any time soon.

Well, it ain’t Agamemnon.
It is on the first floor of the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, as part of a rather amazing collection of prehistoric * material, including nice Cycladic pieces and earlier, but in a pair of connected rooms that are more-or-less the stuff Schliemann collected from the shaft graves he excavated at Mycenae.
So the collection is, pretty much beyond dispute, full of Mycenaean objects. A whole whole bunch of tiny delicate gold, looking as new as the day it was made, some rather less well preserved (gold is incorruptible) swords, and a fragment of a boar’s tusk helmet.
And a few rhyton and pots that are themselves famous — the Warrior Vase, prime among them — but I want to come back to that helmet.
Because the Mycenae are pre-historic. They did write, or rather they took account books, but the closest we come to a “history” of them is Greek mythology, and particularly the Homeric cycle written (off the top of my head so don’t quote me!) about four hundred years later.

# Is it true that the "golden mask of Agamemnon" that is on display in the National Archeological Museum in Athens is fake? Is anything genuine about this country?
And oh yeah, those shaft grave are older still. If there was a historical “Trojan War,” the graves Schliemann was digging into were from a good four hundred years earlier than that. Which is par for the course with him: at least he didn’t use dynamite this time.
There is controversy about several of the items Schliemann collected. He was pretty much all about controversy. Bragging about stealing from the Turks by hiding the “jewels of Helen” in his young wife’s things… (a story he made up after the fact, at that). So it has been suggested that he may have reworked some of the items to make them look more spectacular.
This is not to cast doubt on the bulk of the collection. There are just too many items there, and too many of them would be all but impossible to fake today, much less in Schliemann’s time. And you really have to visit the museum in person to understand just how much there is there, and how fine and detailed the workmanship is. If he had every goldsmith in Athens working away at it he still couldn’t have faked a hundredth of it, and that’s just the gold items alone.
Aggy’s mask is famous, though. We always like faces, because they seem to speak to us from across the ages. The Fayum portraits have captivated generations, even if there’s some strong evidence that many were mass-produced and not exactly a portrait of the deceased (“Hey, add a little black hair and a mustache on #14, will you? I just talked to the widow.”)
And people are split. Even then, it seemed a little too good to be true. It also is different from other death masks of the same period and circumstance. Some have carried this further and suggested that it was heavily reworked to fit Schliemann’s Germanic preconceptions of a Warrior-King.

Guided, for a first visit. The small-group National Archaeological Museum tour runs two hours with a licensed live guide, is offered in nine languages including English, German, French and Spanish, and costs from €59 per person with the museum ticket included. ## National Archaeological Museum Athens tickets: guided tour or audio guide, and the Tuesday trap
### Opening hours and best time to visit
The National Archaeological Museum Athens has no weekly closing day, but it does have a weekly trap. Every Tuesday, in both seasons, the doors do not open until 13:00. In the summer season, which runs from 4 May to 15 November, the hours are Wednesday to Monday 8:00 to 20:00 and Tuesday 13:00 to 20:00, with last admission at 19:30. In the winter season, from mid-November to early May, they are Wednesday to Monday 8:30 to 15:30, last admission 15:00, and again Tuesday 13:00 to 20:00. Tuesday is therefore the one winter day with an evening opening and the one summer day with no morning. A Tuesday 10 am plan, in any season, means three hours in the cafe garden waiting for the doors.
Ticket sales end 30 minutes before closing and staff begin clearing the galleries 20 minutes before, so a winter afternoon visit needs to start by 13:00 to be worth the ticket. The museum closes on 25 and 26 December, 1 January, 25 March, 1 May and Orthodox Easter Sunday. It also warns that individual galleries can close without notice for essential work, with no refund, which is one more argument for not leaving the visit to your last afternoon.
The quiet slot is the first hour after opening on a weekday, 8:00 in summer and 8:30 in winter. Headout's own private-tour page suggests 8 to 10 am for the same reason. The Mycenaean gallery is the first room off the lobby and fills first, so go there straight away and leave the sculpture circuit, which is long, for later. In summer the opening until 20:00 gives a second window: arrive at 17:00 and you still have three hours, which is enough for the route below. Booked ticket holders get priority access at the entrance, which the museum states in its own visit regulation. A booked ticket does not make the galleries emptier.

## National Archaeological Museum Athens tickets: guided tour or audio guide, and the Tuesday trap
### Getting there
The National Archaeological Museum Athens address is 44 Patission Street (officially 28th of October Street), 10682 Athens, about 25 minutes on foot north of Syntagma Square by our estimate, up Panepistimiou and Patission. The museum names two metro stations: Victoria, roughly seven or eight minutes on foot, and Omonia, roughly ten to twelve. Trolleybuses 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13 and 14 stop outside on Patission, and a long list of city buses does too. There is no parking at the museum. The nearest private car parks are on Bouboulinas Street, Zaimi Street and Alexandras Avenue.
From the Acropolis it is about 2.5 kilometres, a 30 to 35 minute walk that nobody enjoys in July. Take the metro from Akropoli to Omonia instead and walk the last ten minutes. The nearest of our other museum pages is the Hellenic Motor Museum, about three minutes away by our estimate, which is a different afternoon altogether if you are travelling with someone who has had enough of marble. The Museum of Cycladic Art and the Benaki are both a walk of around 22 minutes to the south-east in Kolonaki, and the Numismatic Museum about 17 minutes, so a museum day on foot is possible if you start here early.

## National Archaeological Museum Athens tickets: guided tour or audio guide, and the Tuesday trap
### What to see: highlights
*   **Mask of Agamemnon, Room 4.** The first gallery off the lobby holds the gold death masks from the shaft graves of Grave Circles A and B at Mycenae, 16th century BC, with the grave stelae at the entrance, the gold tableware, signet rings and inlaid daggers, the Linear B tablets and the Warrior Vase. The mask known as Agamemnon's comes from Grave V of Circle A. It is the reason most people buy National Archaeological Museum Athens tickets, and it is the room to see before the groups arrive.  
*   **Cycladic harpist, Room 6.** Two marble musicians from Keros, the harpist and the aulos player, stand at the entrance with the largest Cycladic female figure found so far and the folded-arm figurines from Naxos, Syros, Amorgos and Sifnos. Five thousand years old and still the most modern-looking objects in the building.  
*   **Artemision Zeus or Poseidon, Room 15.** An early Classical bronze lifted from the sea off Cape Artemision on Euboea, striding, arm back, and missing the object that would settle whether he threw a thunderbolt or a trident. The museum calls it one of the rarest bronze works to survive. The Eleusis relief is in the same room.  
*   **Jockey of Artemision, Room 34.** A Hellenistic bronze racehorse at full stretch with a boy rider, from the same stretch of sea, placed at the end of the sculpture circuit so that the walk through the kouroi, the stele of Hegeso and the Diadoumenos builds up to it.  
*   **Antikythera Mechanism, Room 38.** The bronze geared device from the Antikythera shipwreck, dated 150 to 100 BC, which the museum's brochure describes as the oldest surviving portable astronomical and calendrical mechanical computer. It is shown in the Metalwork collection with the other finds from the wreck, and it is small, so give it time.

Title: National Archaeological Museum Athens: What to Actually Look For (2026 Guide)

Tour groups hit the Mycenaean gold rooms by 10 a.m. The museum opens at 8 a.m. in summer (Tuesday from 1 p.m. — avoid Tuesday mornings). Arrive at 8 and go straight to Room 4. You'll have the Mask of Agamemnon to yourself for about 20 minutes.
The Antikythera Mechanism — a 2,100-year-old astronomical calculator with 30 interlocking gears — is in Room 38 upstairs. Roughly 80% of visitors never make it to the second floor. The corroded fragments look unremarkable; the working reconstruction next to them is one of the most extraordinary objects in the building.
Full admission is €15, reduced €8. Free on the first Sunday of the month from November to March (not in summer). Photography without flash is permitted throughout. The museum is at Patission 44 — nearest metro is Omonia (Lines 1 and 2), then a 10-minute walk north along Patission Street.
The National Archaeological Museum is the largest archaeological museum in Greece and one of the most significant in the world. Its collection spans roughly 7,000 years of Greek history, from the Neolithic period through late antiquity. That scale is also the problem.
When every room contains world-class objects with three-line placards, everything starts to blur. A Mycenaean gold cup from 1500 BCE sits three meters from a Roman marble portrait from 200 CE with almost identical presentation. Without context, the eye stops distinguishing.
The approach that works is selective. This is not a place to see everything — it's a place to understand six specific things very well. Choose those objects. Know their stories before you walk in. When you stand in front of the Mask of Agamemnon or the Artemision Bronze with the full story already loaded, the experience becomes something different: a confirmation of something you almost already knew, delivered in three dimensions at 1:1 scale.

**Room 4** holds the Mycenaean gold collection — funeral goods excavated by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876 from the royal shaft graves at **Mycenae**, the fortified Bronze Age palace city in the Peloponnese. The room contains extraordinary objects: inlaid daggers, ceremonial drinking cups, amber jewelry. In the center case, behind glass, is a hammered-gold funeral mask the size of a human face.
Schliemann sent a telegram to the King of Greece when he found it: *'I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon.'* The name has never left the object.
The mask almost certainly does not show Agamemnon. The man depicted was buried around 1550–1500 BCE, and Agamemnon — if he existed — would have lived around 1250 BCE. The mask predates any plausible Trojan War by 250 to 300 years. What it does show is a specific man: heavy beard, mustache, a face of middle age, eyes closed, features pressed from a single sheet of hammered gold by someone who knew this face well enough to render it with personality rather than convention. He was powerful enough to be buried wearing 450 grams of gold, and someone cared about his face enough to record it.
The Mycenaean civilization left almost no narrative texts — Linear B has been deciphered, but the tablets are administrative records, not history. This mask and the objects around it in Room 4 are among the few things from that world that carry the weight of individual human presence.
Get short, interactive stories that make each place easier to remember while you travel.
Near the end of the sculpture gallery, a bronze figure stands in mid-throw. Both arms are fully extended — one forward, one swept back — in a pose of suspended force. The figure is 2.09 meters tall, clearly divine, and dated to approximately **460 BCE**, the Early Classical period just before the Parthenon.
The statue was found in 1926 and 1928 in the sea off **Cape Artemision**, on the northern tip of the island of Euboea — the same waters where the Greeks and Persians fought a major naval battle in 480 BCE. It had been on a ship that sank during Roman-era transport.

The debate that has never been resolved: if the god is holding a **trident**, he's Poseidon. If he's holding a **thunderbolt**, he's Zeus. Both weapons would have been thin bronze rods, long since lost. The right hand is open. Art historians have been arguing about the width of that grip for ninety years.
What is unambiguous is the technical achievement. The figure's weight rests on one foot, the torso is rotated nearly 90 degrees, and the extended arms create a span of over two meters — all in solid bronze, all in perfect balance. Whoever cast this in the 5th century BCE was working at a level that would not be matched in Europe for roughly 1,500 years. The **Jockey of Artemision**, nearby — a small boy on a full-speed galloping horse, his face straining with effort, circa 150 BCE — came from the same underwater site and is equally worth stopping for.
In 1900, a sponge-diving boat caught in a storm off the small island of **Antikythera** — between Crete and the Peloponnese — dropped anchor in a bay and sent divers down to wait out the weather. One of them surfaced with pieces of bronze. What followed was the first major underwater archaeological excavation in history.
The **Antikythera shipwreck** was a large Roman-era cargo vessel, probably carrying looted Greek art from the Aegean back to Italy. The haul included life-size statues, glassware, pottery, and one object that would not be fully understood for another century.
The most visible survivor, displayed in the sculpture galleries, is the **Youth of Antikythera** — a nearly complete bronze figure, 1.96 meters tall, his right arm extended as if he once held something (an apple? a ball? scholarly opinion is divided). The original eyes were glass or stone, now missing. What remains has a quality of arrested presence — someone caught mid-moment, not posed. It is one of the finest surviving bronzes from the 4th century BCE.
Take the staircase to the **second floor**. In **Room 38**, behind glass, are fragments of corroded bronze that look like they belong in a geology collection. The placard explains what they are: the remains of a **mechanical astronomical calculator** built approximately 100 BCE.

The **Antikythera Mechanism** contained at least 30 interlocking bronze gear wheels inside a hand-sized wooden box, operated by a hand crank. Turning the crank moved pointers on circular dials on the front and back faces. The front dial tracked the positions of the sun and moon in the zodiac. The back dials tracked the **Metonic cycle** (the 19-year alignment of the lunar and solar calendars), the **Saros cycle** (an 18-year eclipse prediction cycle), and a games calendar used to schedule the Olympic and Panhellenic festivals.
In plain terms: it predicted where the sun and moon would be on any future date and told you when the next eclipse would occur, 18 years in advance, correctly.
The nearest comparable European technology — mechanical astronomical clocks using similar gear trains — does not appear until the **14th century CE**. The Antikythera Mechanism is roughly 1,400 years ahead of anything else in the record. A working reconstruction, built by University College London researchers in 2021, stands next to the fragments. The reconstruction rotates. It is the most useful exhibit in the museum, and most visitors never see it.
**Room 48** holds the Thera frescoes — wall paintings from **Akrotiri**, the Bronze Age settlement on Santorini buried when the Thera volcano erupted around 1600 BCE. Akrotiri was a sophisticated trading city: multi-story buildings, indoor plumbing, elaborate painted walls. The ash preserved it for 3,600 years before excavation began in 1967.
The frescoes are remarkable on two grounds. First, the color: the sealed ash environment preserved the mineral pigments at near-full intensity. A painting of swallows in flight from 1600 BCE looks like it was made recently. Second, the subjects: the Akrotiri painters depicted daily life with unusual warmth and specificity. The **'Boxing Children' fresco** shows two boys in gloves sparring, their faces unposed and concentrated. The **'Spring fresco'** shows swallows over red lilies growing from rocky outcrops — a landscape painting, which is a genuinely unusual genre in ancient art.

The people of Akrotiri appear to have evacuated before the eruption — no human remains have been found in the ruins, and no gold was left behind. Someone warned them. Who gave the warning and how the population survived is unknown. The paintings they left on their walls are in Room 48.
**The ceramic galleries** (Rooms 49–56, on the ground and upper floors) are excellent by any specialist standard but visually repetitive without prior knowledge of Greek vase-painting conventions. Spend 10 minutes here rather than 45 unless ceramics are your specific interest.
**The Egyptian and Near Eastern collection** on the ground floor is a curiosity — these objects came to Athens through ancient trade — but is secondary to the Greek material. A glance is enough.
**The audio guide** (€5 extra) covers the Mycenaean and sculpture galleries well, but does not meaningfully cover the Antikythera Mechanism or the Akrotiri frescoes. For Rooms 38 and 48, the display placards are more informative. Skip the guide for those rooms.
**The museum shop**, near the exit, sells a working mini-replica of the Antikythera Mechanism gear model — one of the more legitimate souvenirs available in Athens, since the actual object is housed here. It is not available in most tourist shops.
**When to visit?** In June, the museum is open daily **8 a.m. to 8 p.m.** (Tuesdays from 1 p.m.). Lightest crowds are at opening and the hour before closing. Tour groups typically land between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. The building is fully air-conditioned — one of the few central Athens attractions that is genuinely comfortable at midday in summer, when outdoor temperatures regularly reach 34–36°C.
**How long?** The six-object approach in this guide takes about **2 to 2.5 hours** at a comfortable pace, including time to read placards and move between floors. A full survey of the museum takes 4 to 5 hours and is genuinely tiring. If you are visiting with children, Room 4 (Mycenaean gold) and Room 15 (the Artemision Bronze) are the most immediately striking for first-timers.

**How to get there?** The museum is at **Patission 44**, about 1 km north of Omonia Square. From **Omonia metro** (Lines 1 and 2), walk north along Patission Street — about 10 minutes. From Exarcheia, the neighborhood directly east, it is a 5-minute walk west along Stournari Street. Combining the museum with lunch in Exarcheia is a natural pairing: Kallidromiou Street market and the cafes around Exarcheia Square are 10 minutes on foot from the museum entrance.

Given the lack of other stylistic evidence to compare the masks to, the biggest problem with resolving the question is that it’s difficult to authenticate metal objects. Or rather, there are ways in which their authenticity might be ruled out but not really ruled in. It would be possible, for example, to chemically analyze the mask to see if its composition matches that of more securely identified Mycenaean gold items. However, the mask might have been made from scraps of ancient gold, giving it the same composition. On top of that, museums tend to be generally unenthusiastic about the prospect of establishing that their most prized holdings may be forgeries, so there’s been little activity in that direction.
So, then, the question has been raised based on plausible but not overwhelmingly strong evidence, and there’s no particular urgency on the part of the museum holding the mask to respond to those charges. Don’t look for this to be settled any time soon.

The building is a neoclassical design by the architect L.
